newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo couldn't replace trader despite suspicion.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo couldn't replace trader despite suspicion.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp grew leery of its powerful top copper trader after a huge deal more than three years ago that broke company rules, but it could not replace him, a Sumitomo manager testified on Monday.

In the third session of one-time Sumitomo copper chief Yasuo Hamanaka's fraud and forgery trial, defense lawyers continued grilling a Sumitomo manager on what they suggested were inadequate checks and controls at the giant trade house.

Hamanaka has pleaded guilty to charges of fraud and forgery in secret deals that Sumitomo blames for a massive $2.6 billion loss. His lawyers hope to convince judges that Sumitomo's laxity also contributed to the loss and that they should therefore be lenient when sentencing the defendant.
The combined fraud and forgery charges carry a maximum penalty of 15 years in jail.

In Monday's testimony, Yoshio Takeuchi of Sumitomo's credit control department said the trade house became suspicious after a Hong Kong subsidiary extended credit of 31.2 billion yen in September 1993 in connection with a Hamanaka transaction. The amount far exceeded company limits, he said.
"It greatly deviated from internal rules," Takeuchi told the court. "The control section issued a warning (to the Hong Kong office) and asked them why and how it happened."

Takeuchi said Hamanaka defended the transaction as necessary for a large copper warrant deal, to take ownership of physical metal. Takeuchi did not indicate if any internal probes were subsequently made or if any reprimands were handed out.
He said, however, the deal prompted Sumitomo to reestablish a team inside its non-ferrous metals division to monitor transactions. A prior team in the division had been disbanded in April 1993.
"Because of the incident in Hong Kong, we thought it was necessary to strengthen controls in the non-ferrous division," he said.
Takeuchi also testified that Sumitomo tried to groom a successor to Hamanaka in the early 1990s but his reputation for trading prowess made him difficult to replace .
"Sumitomo had nobody who had more knowledge about metal trading than Hamanaka. They viewed him as a very able trader," Takeuchi said.
"Hamanaka had too big a presence," he added. "They tried to find someone to replace him and in 1992 sent a precious metal trader to the copper trading team, but he quit Sumitomo."

Takeuchi also said Hamanaka was supposed to report regularly to the credit control section on Sumitomo's copper positions and credit lines to clients, although these reports were sometimes late and Takeuchi's group occasionally had to prod the Hamanaka team to provide information.

Takeuchi said he worked with Hamanaka from June 6 to June 8 of last year, after Hamanaka revealed his off-the-books deals to his superiors, to figure out the amount of his losses and remaining positions.
Judges said during today's proceedings that the fourth hearing in Hamanaka's trial, originally set for March 31, would be rescheduled. --Tokyo Commodity Desk +81-3-3432-7391
